promptText: What is an embedding, in plain terms?
options: A compressed version of a document used only for storage efficiency
A fixed-length list of numbers representing text such that similar-meaning text produces vectors that are close together in that numeric space
A hash of the text used to detect exact duplicates
A summary of the text generated by an LLM
explanation: An embedding is a vector representation designed so that semantic similarity between texts corresponds to geometric closeness between their vectors, even when the texts share no words.

promptText: Why does plain keyword search (like SQL LIKE or a full-text index) often fail to find relevant documents that embeddings would find?
options: Keyword search is slower than vector search in every case
Keyword search matches literal strings, so it fails when a query and a relevant document use different words for the same concept
Keyword search cannot be implemented in Java
Keyword search requires a GPU to run efficiently
explanation: Keyword search matches surface text, not meaning, so it misses relevant content that expresses the same idea with different vocabulary -- exactly the gap embeddings close by capturing semantic similarity.

promptText: What is the purpose of the 'pooling' step in the embedding pipeline?
options: It normalizes the input text to lowercase before tokenization
It collapses the many context-aware token vectors produced by the Transformer layers into a single fixed-length vector representing the whole input
It removes stop words from the input before embedding
It compresses the final vector using quantization
explanation: After self-attention layers produce a context-aware vector per token, pooling (commonly mean pooling or a CLS-token) collapses those many vectors into the one fixed-length output vector the model returns.

promptText: What does cosine similarity measure between two embedding vectors?
options: The straight-line (Euclidean) distance between the two points
The angle between the two vectors, ignoring their magnitude
The number of shared dimensions with identical values
The total token count difference between the two source texts
explanation: Cosine similarity captures the angle between two vectors regardless of their length, which is why it works consistently even when comparing texts of very different lengths.

promptText: What typically happens when text submitted for embedding exceeds the model's maximum sequence length?
options: The embedding model automatically summarizes the text first
The request is queued until a larger model becomes available
The text is silently truncated or rejected, meaning content beyond the limit never influences the resulting vector
The embedding model splits the text into multiple vectors automatically and averages them
explanation: Every embedding model has a hard token limit; text beyond it is truncated or rejected depending on the client library, which is a direct, practical reason chunking is mandatory for real documents.

promptText: What is the basic architectural difference between a bi-encoder and a cross-encoder?
options: A bi-encoder requires GPU inference while a cross-encoder can run on CPU
A bi-encoder embeds each text independently for later comparison; a cross-encoder processes both texts together in one pass so attention can compare them directly
A cross-encoder is only used for image embeddings
A bi-encoder can only produce binary (0/1) similarity scores
explanation: Bi-encoders produce independent, pre-computable vectors compared with a cheap similarity function; cross-encoders feed both texts in together for a more accurate but non-precomputable joint score.

promptText: Why must the exact same embedding model be used for both ingesting documents and embedding queries at search time?
options: Using different models is fine as long as both were trained by the same company
Different embedding models produce generally incomparable vector spaces, so comparing vectors from two different models returns arbitrary, irrelevant results with no error thrown
It is only a performance optimization, not a correctness requirement
The vector database enforces this automatically and will reject mismatched vectors
explanation: Vectors from different models (or even different versions) live in unrelated coordinate spaces; similarity search across mismatched models silently returns meaningless rankings, which is why swapping models requires a full re-embedding migration.

promptText: How does Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) differ from simply truncating dimensions off an ordinary embedding model's output?
options: MRL requires storing multiple full-size copies of every vector

MRL trains the model so meaningful information concentrates toward the front of the vector, making several truncated prefixes independently usable, whereas naive slicing of an ordinary model produces an incoherent, badly-degraded vector
MRL only works for image embedding models, not text
MRL and naive truncation produce identical results for any model
explanation: MRL explicitly optimizes truncated prefixes of the vector during training to each perform well independently; a model never trained this way has no guarantee that slicing its output preserves usable structure.

promptText: What is a 'hard negative' in contrastive training, and why does it matter more than a random (easy) negative?
options: A hard negative is a corrupted training example that should be filtered out before training

A hard negative is superficially similar to the anchor but not the correct match, forcing the model to sharpen fine-grained distinctions, whereas easy negatives mostly teach it to separate obviously different topics
A hard negative is simply a negative example with a longer text length
Hard negatives are only used during evaluation, never during training
explanation: Random negatives are usually easy to separate and teach little; hard negatives are deceptively close to the anchor and force the model to learn the finer decision boundaries that actually determine real-world retrieval precision.

promptText: A retrieved passage has very high cosine similarity to a user's query but contains outdated or factually wrong information. What does this reveal about embedding similarity?
options: This should never happen; high similarity guarantees factual correctness
Embeddings capture topical and phrasing similarity, not truth or correctness, since they were trained via contrastive learning on semantic relatedness, not fact-checking
The embedding model must be broken and needs to be re-trained
This only happens with models under 512 dimensions
explanation: Contrastive training optimizes for semantic/topical closeness, not veracity; a passage can be phrased almost identically to the query while being outdated or wrong, which is why similarity alone cannot serve as a correctness signal.

promptText: What is the purpose of the E5 model family's 'query:' and 'passage:' text prefixes?
options: They are purely cosmetic labels with no effect on the resulting vector
They tell the model which encoding mode to use, since E5 is trained asymmetrically to produce better-matched vectors for queries versus documents
They compress the input text to fit within the token limit
They are required only for multilingual queries
explanation: E5 is trained to expect these prefixes so it can encode a short query and a longer passage differently but compatibly; omitting or misapplying them silently degrades retrieval quality without throwing an error.

promptText: Why might a model with a top MTEB average score still perform poorly specifically on your RAG retrieval use case?
options: MTEB scores are randomly generated and carry no signal at all

The average blends many unrelated task types (classification, clustering, STS) with retrieval, so a model can excel elsewhere while being comparatively weak at the asymmetric query-to-passage matching retrieval actually requires
MTEB only evaluates models smaller than 100 million parameters
A high MTEB average always guarantees the best retrieval performance on any domain
explanation: MTEB's overall average is a blend across many task types; for RAG specifically, the retrieval subtask score (and ideally your own domain evaluation) matters far more than the aggregate number.

promptText: Compare int8 quantization and binary quantization of embedding vectors. What is the key trade-off, and how is binary quantization typically used in practice to manage its downside?
options: Both provide identical compression and accuracy; the choice is purely a matter of API availability

Int8 maps each dimension to one of 256 values (roughly 4x smaller, small accuracy loss); binary quantization collapses each dimension to one bit (up to 32x smaller, larger accuracy loss), so binary search is typically paired with a re-scoring step using full-precision vectors on the top candidates
Binary quantization always outperforms int8 in both speed and accuracy with no trade-off
Int8 quantization is only compatible with sparse embeddings, not dense ones
explanation: Int8 quantization offers a moderate compression/accuracy trade-off, while binary quantization is far more aggressive and lossy; production systems typically use binary vectors for fast initial candidate retrieval and re-score the shortlist with full-precision vectors to recover accuracy.

promptText: Why can't a cross-encoder simply replace bi-encoder embedding search entirely, even though cross-encoders are more accurate at scoring relevance?
options: Cross-encoders cannot be used for text, only for images

A cross-encoder requires a full model forward pass per query-document pair since both texts must be present together, making it computationally prohibitive to score against millions of documents in real time -- so it is used only to re-rank a small candidate set already narrowed by a bi-encoder
Cross-encoders cannot be trained with contrastive learning
Cross-encoders always produce lower-quality scores than bi-encoders
explanation: Cross-encoders cannot pre-compute document representations independent of the query, so scoring an entire corpus is computationally infeasible; the standard architecture uses a fast bi-encoder for initial retrieval and a cross-encoder only to re-rank the small shortlist.

promptText: A provider releases embedding model v2 with better public benchmark scores than the v1 model your 5-million-document index currently uses. What is the correct migration approach, and why can't you simply swap the model in configuration?
options: Swap the EmbeddingModel bean in configuration; since both are from the same provider, existing vectors remain valid

Validate v2 against your own labeled evaluation set first, then re-embed the full corpus into a separate new index, run both in parallel to validate quality, and only cut over query-time embedding atomically with the index switch -- because vectors from v1 and v2 are not comparable and public benchmarks may not reflect your domain
Simply average the v1 and v2 vectors for each document to blend the benefits of both models
Delete the v1 index immediately and begin embedding new documents with v2 only, leaving old documents unembedded
explanation: Since different model versions produce incomparable vector spaces, a config swap alone would silently corrupt every similarity ranking; the safe path is evaluating on your own data, building a separate index, validating in parallel, and cutting over the query path atomically with the index switch.
